Question: Should Major League Baseball enact a salary cap?
Answer: No. The only real effect of a salary cap is to artificially restrain player salaries and transfer money from the players to the owners. MLB doesn’t have a competitive balance problem. It has a “several owners who aren’t interested in fielding competitive teams” problem and a salary cap won’t fix that. Also, there’s the small matter that MLB can’t just “enact” it — it would be a mandatory bargaining issue with the players’ union, and the MLBPA is much stronger than the unions in the NHL, NFL and NBA that were basically broken and forced to accept a salary cap.

Question: How do you get to Yankee Stadium from Albany?

The drive is ~2 hours (depending on exactly where you are starting in Albany) and has a $3.84 toll if you have E-Z Pass, and the train ride is ~1 hour and costs around $7/ticket. It’s a 5–10 minute walk to the stadium once you get off the train, and you get to see the youth baseball fields they built on the site where the stadium used to be. A more expensive option with less driving is to take Amtrak from Albany-Rensselaer to NY Penn Station (Moynihan Train Hall). From there, you can walk over to 34th St/Herald Square and take the D train uptown to the 161st St/Yankee Stadium stop or take the 1 train uptown from Penn to 42nd Street, transfer to the S to Grand Central, then take the 4 uptown to 161st St/Yankee Stadium. Question: Is it hard to be homeschooled into my sophomore year of high school? I've been home schooled most of my life.
Answer: Maybe? Homeschooling high school can be difficult for a couple of reasons. For one, that’s an age when relationships between parents and children can become strained. When you’re homeschooling that can make things hard to manage. For another, you’re getting into areas where it’s more difficult (though far from impossible) because you need resources to do lab work in science and are starting to get into advanced (beyond algebra) math. Those can be challenging to manage even for parents who had no problems with earlier grades. There are ways around that, of course; when we were doing biology, we got a friend who’s a veterinarian to come and do dissections with our kids (and several of their friends). Partly because we wanted our kids to get a taste of what college was going to be like, we had them start taking some classes (just 1 at first) at a local community college. That gave them a chance to get used to a different style of instruction and meet new people and really was a good early transition to thinking about things the way they were going to have to do when they actually started college.

Question: I know Judge Juan Merchan was appointed to the bench in 2009 and I understand that the New York Supreme Court term of office is 14 years. Did Judge Merchan run in an election after 2009?
Answer: No. Judge Merchan is an acting Supreme Court Judge. From Wikipedia: The number of justices of the Supreme Court in each New York Supreme Court judicial district (including justices assigned to the Appellate Division) is set forth by the New York State Constitution. Once a decade, the state Legislature may increase the number of justices in any judicial district, but Article VI of the state Constitution sets a population-based cap on the number of justices in each district, based on census data. As a result of the population-based cap, some areas have overloaded courts. New York City has a cap of 171 justices (and only some of the New York Supreme Court justices in New York City serve in trial parts, with others assigned to the Appellate Division or the Appellate Term). As a result, New York City has too few judges to handle New York City's caseload, which is more than 100,000 cases annually; the population-based formula in the state Constitution does not account for the millions of non-resident workers and visitors in the city, nor the 315,000 business associations that operate in the city. To address the imbalance, the New York court system designates other courts' judges (such as those sitting on the lower-level New York City Civil Court, New York City Criminal Court, and New York City Family Court, as well as the statewide New York Court of Claims) as "acting" Supreme Court justices to serve on the New York Supreme Court in New York City. From the Wikipedia article on Merchan: Merchan became a judge in 2006 when New York City mayor Michael Bloomberg appointed him to the New York City Family Court, Bronx County. He remained in that role until 2009. Chief Administrative Judge Ann Pfau appointed Merchan as Acting Justice in the Supreme Court of New York, New York County, Criminal, in 2009, and he has been in that position since that time. Merchan presides over felony criminal trials. His appointed term ends in 2028.

Question: Why do some people think voting in elections is like a vending machine?
Answer: Responding because I think something I said in an earlier answer may have inspired this question. I wish I knew. I think that attitude is a huge problem for a self-governing society, but I really don’t have a good theory on why it happened. I have a little bit of theory of how it happened. In the early days of the US, most politics was relatively local. Most people voted for people they trusted and generally let them run things. As time passed, national politics became more and more significant, but most people still voted based largely on local concerns. I think maybe they felt like they were turning the ship of state, but only by having enough people run to one side of the boat to make it tilt in that direction. At some point, though, people seemed to get the idea that the national government should address their personal concerns. The idea that a candidate should “earn” your vote came in with that. Somehow, instead of voting being “adding your voice to a discussion about who we want operating the government” it became “a way to get what I, personally want” — insert vote, get policy. At least, that’s my general theory of how we got here; I think part of the “why” is the political parties encouraging their most fervent supporters to think that way with ever-more-specific campaign promises, but I don’t think that’s nearly all of it.

Question: Baseball: A runner on 1st base and 1 out. Batter pops a high fly to 2nd. The runner at 1st runs all the way to 3rd, stops and remains. The ump calls infield fly/batter out. The fielder drops the fly ball. Can the runner be forced out at 1st or 2nd?
Answer: No. As soon as the batter-runner is called out, the force is removed. And the batter-runner is out even if the ball is dropped. The bigger problem is that that’s not a situation where the umpire can call an infield fly. From the definitions in the MLB rule book: An INFIELD FLY is a fair fly ball (not including a line drive nor an attempted bunt) which can be caught by an infielder with ordinary effort, when first and second, or first, second and third bases are occupied, before two are out. The pitcher, catcher and any outfielder who stations himself in the infield on the play shall be considered infielders for the purpose of this rule. You could rephrase the question to have runners on first and second and have them both advance only one base; it would be a valid case for the infield fly at that point, and neither runner could be forced out once it was called. In fact, both runners could be standing between bases waiting to see what happens when the ball is dropped and they still couldn’t be forced if advancing to 2nd and 3rd. They could be put out, but it would be a tag play.

Question: Is an MLB team playing say a hard team to beat like New York Yankees 11 times, in their division unfair compared to another team in the same division playing another baseball team 11 times that is known for finishing last each year?
Answer: Yes, but also no. The divisions are set up and seldom change, usually only when new teams are added to the league. It’s arguably not fair that each team in the league doesn’t play each other team the same number of times. On the other hand, the rules that set the schedule are agreed to by all the teams, so in another way it’s hard to say they’re not fair — everyone plays by the same rules. It’s also not true that there are teams “known for finishing last each year” over a longer time period. The Yankees went through a period from 1965–1973 when they finished higher than fourth in the standings exactly once. The Orioles over the same period played in the post season six times and finished lower than 2nd in the standings just once. If you looked at the last several years, you’d see the opposite situation but the Orioles have built a strong young team and are now fighting it out with the Yankees for first place.
